zh_summary: @SawyerMerritt: NHTSA proposed rules to remove federal barriers for autonomous vehicles without steering wheels or pedals, such as Tesla's Cybercab, including dropping manual turn signal control requirements.
en_summary: @SawyerMerritt: NHTSA proposed rules to remove federal barriers for autonomous vehicles without steering wheels or pedals, such as Tesla's Cybercab, including dropping manual turn signal control requirements.
text:
NHTSA announced today that they are proposing new rules aimed at removing U.S. federal regulatory barriers for autonomous vehicles without steering wheels or pedals, such as @Tesla's Cybercab.

The proposed changes include:
• Eliminating requirements for manually operated turn signal controls in vehicles without steering wheels or pedals: "NHTSA has concluded that the self-canceling and manually operated control requirements in the current standard are unnecessary for turn signal operating units that are installed on vehicles without manually operated driving controls."

• Allowing autonomous driving systems to control turn signals, hazard lights, and high/low beams without traditional driver-operated switches.

• Removing certain dashboard indicator requirements for turn signals and high beams in vehicles without manual driving controls.

• Allowing optional cyan-colored exterior lights to indicate when a vehicle is operating autonomously, with standardized requirements for their placement, brightness, and operation.

• Eliminating outdated restrictions on vertical headlight arrangements, giving automakers greater design flexibility.

• Allowing modern integrated headlights to be tested at manufacturer-specified voltages rather than requiring 12.8 volts.

NHTSA says the changes are intended to eliminate unnecessary regulatory barriers, reduce costs, and enable innovation without compromising vehicle safety.

en_summary: @aleabitoreddit: $NVDA Jensen Huang told CNBC a memory oversupply by 2029 is unlikely because you can always use more memory, citing LPDDR use in data centers, rebutting a Korean view of a 2029 red ocean.
text:
$NVDA Jensen Huang: Surplus of memory supply is unlikely by 2029. 

The CNBC question referenced a Korean newspaper opinion on $KOSPI / Samsung / SK Hynix that predicted "new supply will leave the memory sector a red ocean in 2029."

"One of the things that's really great about memory is that you can always use more of it", Jensen said, citing LPDDR usage in DCs.  And responded "I don't think so" in terms of possibilities of oversupply in 2029. 

Just my personal opinion, Nvidia probably has the most visibility in the entire industry. 

Especially around supply procurement and emerging capacity, given they're the ones leading all the architectural shifts. 

On durability, you have Samsung already allocated majority of capacity into 2031 from SED and hyperscalers like $GOOGL are already reportedly securing memory LTAs into 2035 from KeyBanc. 

Yet there's endless "it's all over" sentiment on memory now. I'd probably trust Jensen's opinion here.
